title: Functions Part 1: Creating and Calling Functions
summary: Introduces functions as named, reusable blocks of instructions, using a house-robot 'get milk' routine; covers the declaration syntax, calling with name plus parentheses, indentation style, and swapping alert for console.log while testing.

concepts.heading: Why functions exist
points: A fixed sequence of instructions (a robot walking to a shop, buying milk and returning, written as a long list of alert calls) would otherwise have to be retyped every time it is needed.
A function packages that sequence under a name so one short call repeats the whole thing. This keeps code DRY (do not repeat yourself).
A computer only does what it is told, so the function must contain every low-level step.

concepts.heading: Declaring a function
points: Syntax: the function keyword, then the name, then a pair of round brackets, then curly braces holding the body.
The opening { marks where the instructions start and the closing } where they end; everything between runs when the function is called.
The structure parallels a variable: var name = value creates a container, function name() { ... } creates a named block of behaviour.
Function names follow the variable naming rules and camelCase convention (getMilk); a name cannot start with a digit.
The brackets are empty here; parameters come in the next lesson.
Style: indent every line inside the braces so the parent/child structure is visible. A function declaration's closing brace is not followed by a semicolon.

concepts.heading: Declaring versus calling
points: Declaring defines what the function does and runs nothing.
Calling is writing getMilk(); : the name, empty parentheses and a semicolon, with no function keyword and no braces.
On a call the engine finds the matching declaration and executes its body in order.

concepts.heading: alert versus console.log
points: Clicking through many alerts while testing is tedious; replace them with console.log() (in the editor use find-and-replace, Replace All).
alert is visible to every visitor of the page. console.log output only appears in the developer console and is meant for debugging and inspecting values.
The function works identically either way.

code_examples.caption: A function with the milk-run instructions, called twice

pitfalls: Writing getMilk without parentheses does not run it.
Starting a function name with a number, or using spaces.
Putting a semicolon after the closing brace of a declaration is unnecessary.
(Extra) Calling a function never changes anything until the declaration has been read; declaring alone produces no output.

playground.coverage: Has the define/call distinction, a getMilk log sequence, calling twice, notes on brackets and reasons for functions.
gaps_and_ideas: Add the contrast with alert (user-visible) versus console.log (developer-only) and a find-and-replace step as a task.
Add the naming rules recap: camelCase, no leading digit.
Explore demo idea: a small robot grid where getMilk() animates the moves, so calling once vs twice is visible.
